Logging to local or network paths detected
 Mandatory 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\log4Net.xml

Explanation

Logging to local or network paths detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, prefer Application Insights/App Service logging. If filesystem logs are required, write to a mounted Azure Files share configured via storage mounts and Key Vault secrets.

Logging APIs that write to disk might not work on Azure App Service or Container.

Use logging that stores logs in locations outside of the host unless its specifically required by your app. You can also use logging capabilities embedded in Azure, such as Azure App Service logging or Application Insights.

For migrating to AKS, use LogMonitor tool that can capture logs written to files, the console, or write logs and redirect them to Azure.

Explanation

Your application has local or network IO operations.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move persistent I/O to storage mounts (Azure Files/UNC). Keep local writes to temp only; connect to external dependencies via private endpoints/VNet to reduce latency.

IO operations outside of the application folder might not be available on Azure App Service. Review and ensure IO APIs are attempting to access paths that will be available when your app is running on App Service sandbox. If you choose the containerized hosting option, your scenario still might be broken or have scalability issues.

Possible solutions:
1. Files that the application needs can be deployed with the application or put in Azure Storage. You can use Azure Storage File Shares as a drop-in replacement for on-premises file share.
2. Other services that the application depends on might need to be migrated to Azure, this way you will get the benefit of lower latency in the cloud.
3. If your application needs to depend on services that run on-premise, you can connect your Azure and local networks with ExpressRoute, Hybrid Connections, or VPN solutions.

Local OS environment access detected
 Potential 1
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Global.asax.csLine 42

Explanation

Local OS environment access detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, Read config via App Settings or App Configuration; avoid machine‑specific environment APIs. Persist environment setup via install scripts when needed.

When running in Azure App Service environment, your application can read environment variables that you define in App Service settings. Using environment API other than reading environment variables might indicate that your application depends on some local machine's features and might be broken on App Service sandbox or not scale well. Review your scenarios and either refactor them to be more cloud friendly or choose the option in App Service to host your application in the sandbox for Windows Container Web Apps.

If you choose to use other Azure hosting options such as Azure Container Apps (ACA) or Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), environment APIs might work, however scaling still might be an issue.
Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected
 Potential 3
FilePosition
src\eShopLegacyMVC\Web.config

Explanation

Session state stored in-proc or in local process is detected.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, move session to Azure Cache for Redis or Cosmos DB. In-proc session impedes scale-out; Managed Instance does not change session semantics.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

In-proc or local process stored session state not immediately prevents an application from working in Azure, however, is not recommended because it would make scaling the Azure App Service or Azure Kubernetes Service more difficult.

Azure provides multiple ways to store session state in a scalable way using Azure Cache for Redis, Azure Cosmos DB or other services.

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience
 Optional 3
FilePosition
eShopLegacy.Utilities\eShopLegacy.Utilities.csproj
eShopPorted\eShopPorted.csproj

Explanation

Upgrade to newer target framework to get better cloud experience.

If you are targeting Managed Instance on Azure App Service, validate on .NET Framework 4.8 or move to .NET 10. Persist any runtime prerequisites via install scripts; test in staging before production.

While if targeting other Azure compute services:

Application targeting .NET framework lower than 4.7.1 might missing features that would be needed for some cloud scenarios like scaling or getting secrets from secure external sources.

Azure App Service runs apps on .NET Framework 4.8 or .NET Framework 3.5. Apps running on on .NET Framework versions older than .NET Framework 4.8 could have potential compatibility issues. It is recommended to test your application running on .NET Framework 4.8. Note that it is not necessary to re-target to .NET Framework 4.8, only to validate that the app correctly runs on that version of .NET Framework.

In the long term it is also recommended to upgrade your application to latest supported .NET 8+ which would significantly increase performance of your application. Use tools like .NET Upgrade Assistant to help with upgrading your application to newer .NET.

Deprecated Remoting & Serialization
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy .NET Remoting, BinaryFormatter, and related serialization APIs that are deprecated and removed for security reasons. Remoting provided distributed object communication but had significant security vulnerabilities. Migrate to gRPC, HTTP APIs, or modern serialization (System.Text.Json, protobuf).
Legacy Configuration System
 Mandatory 2
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy XML-based configuration system (app.config/web.config) that has been replaced by a more flexible configuration model in .NET Core. The old system was rigid and XML-based. Migrate to Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration with JSON/environment variables; use System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager NuGet package as interim bridge if needed.
ASP.NET Framework (System.Web)
 Mandatory 4
FilePosition

Explanation

Legacy ASP.NET Framework APIs for web applications (System.Web.*) that don't exist in ASP.NET Core due to architectural differences. ASP.NET Core represents a complete redesign of the web framework. Migrate to ASP.NET Core equivalents or consider System.Web.Adapters package for compatibility.

Data Storage & External Services

The legacy MVC application configures a SQL Server LocalDB connection in Web.config; the ported application configures SQL Server through Entity Framework Core and DefaultConnection settings. Both persist catalog items, brands, and types. Application Insights and log4net provide diagnostics; no additional external APIs, caches, or message brokers were identified.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • The MVC 5 and ASP.NET Core projects use separate service and persistence implementations while modeling the same catalog domain.
  • Autofac modules select either mock catalog data or database-backed services from application configuration.
  • The legacy application combines MVC pages and Web API endpoints in one web application.

DTOs & Contracts

CatalogItem, CatalogBrand, and CatalogType are service-level domain entities used in views and API responses. The FilesController.BrandDTO classes (one per web project) define a mutable brand projection used by the binary serialization flow. PaginatedItemsViewModel wraps catalog list results for MVC views. No gateway-level aggregation DTO, OpenAPI specification, protobuf schema, or GraphQL schema was identified. The applications use JSON for ordinary MVC/Web API results and a shared binary serializer for the files endpoint.

Communication Patterns

Communication is synchronous HTTP from clients to each web application, followed by direct in-process controller-to-service calls and synchronous database operations. No service discovery, API gateway, inter-service calls, message broker, retry policy, circuit breaker, or configured request timeout was found. Transport security and authentication/authorization are not configured in the inspected application routes and configuration; no TLS or access-control middleware/attributes were identified.

Core Business Workflows

The application supports browsing and maintaining an online catalog of products, brands, and product types. Catalog data can be served from a mock catalog or from the configured database.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
CatalogItemCatalogA product offered in the catalog, including its stock and image informationAssociated with one CatalogBrand and one CatalogType
CatalogBrandCatalogA brand used to group catalog productsCan be associated with multiple CatalogItems
CatalogTypeCatalogA product type/category used to classify catalog productsCan be associated with multiple CatalogItems

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
eShopLegacyMVCCatalogCatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogTypeSQL Server or mock catalog data
eShopPortedCatalogCatalogItem, CatalogBrand, CatalogTypeSQL Server or mock catalog data

Both applications independently implement the catalog context. No cross-context service communication or shared remote source of truth was identified.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Browse the catalog

  1. A user requests the catalog list and may provide page size and page index.
  2. The catalog controller delegates to the catalog service.
  3. The service retrieves the total item count and a page of catalog items with their brand and type.
  4. The application derives image links and returns a paginated view.
  5. Selecting an item loads its details; an unknown identifier returns not found.

Workflow 2: Maintain a catalog item

  1. A user opens the create or edit form; lookup brands and types are supplied for selection.
  2. The user submits the catalog item form.
  3. The controller checks the submitted model state. If invalid, the form is returned with lookup values; if valid, the service creates or updates the item.
  4. A successful write returns the user to the catalog list.
  5. Deletion is confirmed through a separate form and the item is removed by the catalog service.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no cross-service data aggregation or composition flows. Each application obtains catalog, brand, and type information from its own catalog service implementation, which uses either mock data or its own database context. No remote-service fallback behavior was identified.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant User participant Controller as "Catalog Controller" participant Service as "Catalog Service" participant Data as "Catalog Data Store" User->>Controller: Browse catalog page Controller->>Service: Request item page Service->>Data: Read total and page of items Data-->>Service: Catalog items with lookup data Service-->>Controller: Paginated catalog result Controller-->>User: Render catalog view User->>Controller: Submit catalog item Controller->>Controller: Check model state alt Model is valid Controller->>Service: Create or update item Service->>Data: Save catalog change Data-->>Service: Save completed Service-->>Controller: Operation completed Controller-->>User: Redirect to catalog else Model is invalid Controller-->>User: Return form with validation errors end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Catalog-item forms use model validation before writes. Name is required; Price must be within the configured range and use at most two decimal places; stock and reorder quantities are range-limited.
  • Catalog item creation in the legacy MVC application obtains an identifier from its HiLo sequence generator. The ported service persists the item through its configured data context.
  • Mock-data settings choose between a sample in-memory catalog and the database-backed service; customization-data settings determine how seed data is supplied.
  • There are no documented catalog state transitions, approval process, or price calculation workflow.
  • Catalog writes use synchronous ORM save operations. No explicit audit trail, cross-service transaction, or business authorization rule was identified.

Version & Compatibility Risks

The ported project targets .NET Framework 4.6.1 while using ASP.NET Core 2.2 and EF Core 2.2, both legacy versions. The primary MVC project targets .NET Framework 4.7.2 and uses MVC 5 and EF6; these components require compatibility review during a framework upgrade. Some package versions differ between the legacy and ported projects, notably Autofac and Newtonsoft.Json.

  • The solution maintains separate MVC 5 / Web API 2 and ASP.NET Core 2.2 stacks.
  • Both Entity Framework 6 and EF Core are present, with SQL Server provider dependencies in the ported project.
  • Application Insights has multiple framework-specific collector and telemetry dependencies.
  • No central package management file or test-scoped package dependency was found in the solution.

Caching Strategy

No distributed or in-process query cache, cache provider, or explicit cache-aside strategy was identified. The mock implementations hold sample data in application memory when mock data is enabled; this is the configured default in the ported app.

Each web application has its own context, ORM setup, and database configuration, but both represent the same catalog domain with equivalent entity sets. No cross-service database access or data aggregation between the applications was identified. Reads and writes occur directly through the local catalog service and its context; the legacy application additionally uses SQL Server sequences to generate identifiers.
